Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD) has been one of the top-performing stocks in 2026, clocking impressive gains of over 120% as of this writing, and the good news is that it can deliver further gains to investors thanks to an acceleration in growth.

AMD released its third-quarter results on Nov. 3, and the stock soared the following day. Let's see why that was the case and check how much upside this fast-growing semiconductor stock could deliver by the end of the decade.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: AMD.
AMD's data center business has supercharged its growth

AMD's Q3 revenue increased 45% year over year to $13.4 billion. The company's non-GAAP earnings per share of $2.09 increased by 74% from the year-ago period. AMD's data center business was the primary driver of its impressive growth, with the segment's revenue nearly doubling year over year to a record $8.5 billion.

It is worth noting that AMD's revenue and earnings easily exceeded Wall Street's expectations. The company noted healthy demand for its Epyc server processors and Instinct data center graphics cards. The good news for AMD investors is that the company expects data center revenue to accelerate in the current quarter. What's more, its full-year data center revenue is on track to double from 2025 levels.

Looking ahead, AMD expects the data center segment to account for 80% of its top line in 2027. That implies a major improvement over the previous quarter, when the data center segment produced 64% of AMD's top line. Moreover, the increasing reliance on the data center business is a good sign for AMD, given the ongoing weakness in the personal computer market.

AMD reported an 8% year-over-year decline in its client and gaming segment revenue last quarter to $3.7 billion. Notably, its PC-focused client processor revenue increased 7% from the year-ago period despite a 21% decline in PC industry shipments last quarter. The gaming segment continues to struggle due to the aging gaming console generation. However, the potential arrival of a new generation of gaming consoles next year could lift this segment and complement the healthy growth AMD has been witnessing in data centers.

Importantly, AMD expects significant acceleration in growth despite challenging conditions in the gaming and PC markets. The company expects revenue to increase by 66% year over year in the current quarter, a substantial step up from the 45% growth seen in the previous one.

Goldman Sachs' $675 Target Says AMD's Selloff Went Too Far ©Alexander's Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Goldman Sachs trimmed its AMD price target to $675 from $700 and kept its Buy rating, a target 40% above Tuesday's close.

AMD shares are 28% below their October high after worries over AI spending and Intel's weak PC guidance, even as AMD now expects revenue to grow more than 80% in 2027.

Goldman's target works out to 60x the earnings analysts expect over the next twelve months, near AMD's June peak and well above its 5-year average of 35x.

The target looks reachable in a year if AMD earns what analysts expect for 2027, though that depends on a few AI labs getting their data centers running on time.

Goldman Sachs trimmed its price target on Advanced Micro Devices (AMD:NASDAQ) to $675 from $700 on Wednesday and kept its Buy rating, after AMD's record third quarter. That's 40% above Tuesday's close of $483.90, with the stock 28% below its Oct. 6 closing high.

A rough October for AI chips

AMD's slide began in mid-October, when a selloff in CoreWeave's bonds and questions about OpenAI's revenue revived worries about who pays for the AI build-out.

Then Intel (INTC:NASDAQ) guided fourth-quarter revenue to $15.0 billion to $16.0 billion, with client revenue down more than 20% from the third quarter. AMD lost 11% on Oct. 30 on Intel's PC warning.

Goldman still likes it best

AMD's third-quarter revenue rose 45% year over year to $13.4 billion, and Data Center revenue nearly doubled to $8.5 billion. AMD guided fourth-quarter revenue to about $17 billion, above the roughly $16.2 billion that analysts' full-year forecasts implied going in.

On the call, CEO Lisa Su went further: "we now expect revenue to grow more than 80% in 2027."

Goldman's James Schneider expects the stock "to trade higher following stronger results and guidance which we believe supports our bullish revenue growth outlook for AMD through 2027," and called AMD "our favorite idea in the group." Goldman cut its target because of valuation.

AMD's Data Center Sales Nearly Doubled, but Its Own Stock Rally Just Cost It $1.1 Billion © Kittipong Jirasukhanont from PhonlamaiPhoto's Images and Nickel_Bell from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

AMD beat third-quarter estimates as data center revenue climbed 97% to $8.5 billion, and it guided to about $17 billion of fourth-quarter revenue.

The results also included a $1.1 billion charge for the penny-a-share warrants AMD gave OpenAI and Meta, and that charge grows as AMD's stock rises and its chips ship.

The charge doesn't hit cash or adjusted earnings, but the dilution behind it is real, and free cash flow separately fell to about 4% of revenue as AMD built up inventory.

AMD trades at 42x forward earnings, above its three-year average, so NVIDIA's report later this month and AMD's own fourth quarter are the next tests.

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD:NASDAQ) beat Wall Street's estimates after Tuesday's close, with data center sales nearly doubling.

But the quarter also brought the first bill for the stock AMD promised OpenAI and Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ). Most of that bill comes from AMD's own rally.

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on AMD, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See AMD's Analyst Ratings

What exactly happened

Here's the quarter against Bloomberg's consensus estimates:

Revenue: $13.38 billion, against $13.08 billion expected

Adjusted EPS: $2.09, against $1.97 expected

Data center revenue: $8.5 billion, up 97% from a year earlier and ahead of the $8.19 billion estimate

Fourth-quarter guidance: about $17 billion of revenue, plus or minus 3%

And CEO Lisa Su raised the stakes for next year on the call: "Based on our current visibility, we now expect revenue to grow more than 80% in 2027."

The GAAP results also included a $1.1 billion charge, or $0.66 a share, for the warrants AMD granted OpenAI and Meta. Last quarter, that line was zero.

Under the deals, each company can buy up to 160 million AMD shares at a penny apiece as it rolls out up to 6 gigawatts of AMD chips. The last batch unlocks only if AMD's stock reaches $600. AMD started booking the warrants once its MI450 chips began shipping. CFO Jean Hu said on the call that the charge mostly reflected "the increase in our share price and the changes in the estimated probability of meeting the warrant conditions." AMD's stock rose about 21% last quarter and closed it around $630, above that $600 line.

A bill that grows with the stock

The charge is also set to grow. Hu expects it "to increase as we and our customers progress under this agreement." So every rally and every chip shipment to these two customers adds to it.

title: AMD Stock: Buy, Hold or Sell After 97% AI Data Center Growth?
detail:
AMD Stock: Buy, Hold or Sell After 97% AI Data Center Growth?
Tirthankar Chakraborty
Wed, November 4, 2026 at 12:00 PM MST 3 min read
AMD
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Strong third-quarter performance and a robust fourth-quarter outlook underscore Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.'s AMD growing presence in the rapidly expanding artificial intelligence (AI) market. While rising demand for AMD's advanced data center solutions supports growth, weakness in the gaming segment and valuation concerns remain major apprehensions for investors. Against this backdrop, is AMD stock a buy, hold, or sell now? Let's take a closer look –

AMD's AI Boom Drives Record Growth and Strong Q4 Outlook

AMD is rapidly expanding its business, with third-quarter revenues of $13.38 billion, up 45% year over year and 16% sequentially, according to the company's Nov. 3 press release. The most striking part is the company's Data Center segment, where revenues jumped 97% year over year to a record $8.5 billion, making it the company's primary growth engine. This strong growth was driven by robust demand for AMD's Instinct GPUs, EPYC CPUs, and integrated rack-scale AI systems.

Alongside NVIDIA Corporation NVDA, AMD has now strengthened its position as an alternative supplier of AI infrastructure. Additionally, the company's profitability is growing faster than revenues, indicating positive operating leverage. Its operating income soared 123%, highlighting improving operational efficiency, while non-GAAP earnings per share (EPS) of $2.09 increased 74% year over year. Higher earnings growth could provide meaningful support to AMD's long-term price appreciation.

AMD's fourth-quarter guidance is also strong. The company expects revenues of $17 billion, plus or minus 3%, in the fourth quarter, up 66% year over year and a sequential rise of approximately 27%. This indicates that management is confident that demand for AMD's AI and Data Center products will remain strong.

AMD Stock After Earnings: Buy, Hold or Sell Now?

Strong third-quarter results indicate that AMD is significantly benefiting from the AI infrastructure boom. Its accelerating Data Center business and improving profitability highlight its growing competitiveness in AI infrastructure. Furthermore, management expects revenue growth in the fourth quarter. All these should encourage stakeholders to stay invested.

However, new investors should exercise caution before investing in AMD stock. This is because its strong earnings growth in the third quarter was partially impacted by the weakness in the gaming business. Moreover, the non-GAAP gross margin for the fourth quarter is projected to be approximately 55%, which is slightly less than the reported 56% in the third quarter, signaling potential profitability headwinds.

By Nov. 2, AMD (NASDAQ:AMD) had dropped about 28% from its Oct. 6 record close. Then, after the market closed yesterday, the chipmaker reported that its data center sales had nearly doubled from a year ago. It also forecast fourth-quarter revenue about two-thirds higher than the same quarter last year. The stock rose about 5% in pre-market trading this morning.

Team Rule Breakers recommended AMD in Stock Advisor on Jan. 18, 2024, at $162.67, weeks after the company launched its MI300 AI chips. At the time, AMD's edge over Intel in server processors was well established, and arguably its AI business had barely begun. The stock has roughly tripled since, and it's comfortably ahead of the S&P 500. Team Rule Breakers and Team Hidden Gems have recommended AMD across eight active Motley Fool services, and it has never carried a sell recommendation.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

The second of six Rule Breakers Traits is: Sustainable Competitive Advantage.

This trait asks how a company will keep beating its rivals over the next decade. The advantage can come from a network that gets more valuable as it grows, from patents, from strong leaders, or from rivals that fail to keep up. A company can also have a lasting edge in one business and little or none in another, as AMD's latest report indicates.

Where AMD Outbuilt Intel

For years, AMD and Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) have fought over the processors that run data center servers. AMD builds each processor from several small chips, called chiplets, and joins them in one package. Small chips tend to have fewer defects than one large chip, so more of them come out usable. That can help AMD sell more computing power per dollar.

Under CEO Lisa Su, AMD has steadily won share from Intel by many measures, and Intel's stock fell nearly 29% on Oct. 30 after a weak forecast.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

A Costlier Fight in AI Chips

AMD's position in AI chips is newer and likely less secure. It sells them to OpenAI, Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META), Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), and Oracle (NYSE:ORCL). Management expects AI sales to pass server processor sales for the first time this quarter. But AMD effectively paid to land two of its biggest deals.

It gave OpenAI and Meta warrants for up to 160 million shares each, or about 20% of its share count combined. The warrants are generally tied to how many AMD chips those customers deploy and to AMD's stock price.
